introduction-the-microservices-headache.core: Splitting a monolith into microservices turns function calls into network calls, and each one needs retries, timeouts, load balancing, TLS, auth, metrics and tracing. Implementing that in every service and language leads to inconsistency and duplicated libraries. A service mesh moves these concerns into the infrastructure, usually a proxy beside each service, configured centrally.

first_principles.problem: Fifty services in four languages each implement retries and TLS differently, and an outage is caused by one service's missing timeout.

analogy.title: A building's shared utilities
analogy.story: Instead of every office installing its own generator and security guard, the building provides power and security to all.
analogy.breaks: Utilities are invisible; meshes add latency and operational complexity.

example.title: Library vs mesh
flow: Before: retry logic in Go, Java, Node, Python
After: one retry policy in mesh config

check.q: What problem does a service mesh solve that libraries struggle with?
check.a: Consistent cross-cutting network behaviour (mTLS, retries, telemetry) across many services and languages without code changes.

the-sidecar-proxy-model-istio-envoy.core: In the classic mesh each pod gets an Envoy sidecar injected alongside the app container. iptables rules redirect all inbound and outbound traffic through it, so the app talks plain HTTP to localhost while the sidecar handles mTLS, routing, retries and telemetry. The app needs no changes, but every pod pays for an extra proxy (CPU, memory, latency), and upgrades require restarting pods.

first_principles.problem: A team wants mTLS and traffic policies without touching application code.

analogy.title: A personal assistant for every employee
analogy.story: Each employee's assistant handles their calls, security checks and logs, so employees just work.
analogy.breaks: Assistants are cheap per company; sidecars multiply by pod count.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Every pod now has an Envoy sidecar.

code.text:
kubectl label namespace shop istio-injection=enabled
kubectl rollout restart deploy -n shop
kubectl get pod -n shop -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.containers[*].name}'
# app istio-proxy

check.q: How does the app's traffic reach the sidecar without code changes?
check.a: iptables rules (set up by an init container or CNI) redirect inbound and outbound traffic to the Envoy proxy.

control-plane-vs-data-plane.core: The data plane is the proxies that touch every request. The control plane (istiod, Linkerd's destination and identity services) watches Kubernetes for services, endpoints and mesh policies, computes per-proxy configuration, issues certificates, and pushes it all to the proxies. If the control plane goes down, proxies keep running on their last configuration but can't pick up changes or new certificates.

first_principles.problem: After istiod crashes, existing traffic still flows, but new pods can't communicate.
truths: Decoupling keeps traffic flowing during control-plane outages.
derivation: **Data plane**: proxies on the request path.

analogy.title: Air traffic control vs pilots
analogy.story: Pilots fly the planes (data plane); controllers issue routes and clearances (control plane). If the tower goes quiet, planes in flight continue, but new departures stall.
analogy.breaks: Pilots can improvise; proxies only know their last config.

code.text:
istioctl proxy-status
# NAME              CDS    LDS    EDS    RDS    ISTIOD
# cart-7d9..shop    SYNCED SYNCED SYNCED SYNCED istiod-5f..
# pay-55c..shop     STALE  SYNCED SYNCED SYNCED istiod-5f..

check.q: What happens to mesh traffic if the control plane is unavailable?
check.a: Existing proxies keep forwarding with their last config, but new endpoints, policy changes and certificate rotations stall.

envoy-internals-the-xds-protocol.core: Envoy is configured dynamically through xDS APIs over gRPC streams. LDS sends listeners (ports and filter chains), RDS routes (host and path to cluster), CDS clusters (upstream groups and policies), EDS endpoints (the actual pod IPs) and SDS secrets (TLS certificates). ADS multiplexes them on one stream for ordered updates. A request flows listener → filter chain → HTTP connection manager → route → cluster → endpoint.

first_principles.problem: A route points to a cluster that Envoy doesn't yet know about, causing 503s during deploys.

analogy.title: A building directory updated live
analogy.story: Entrances (listeners) lead to floor guides (routes) to departments (clusters) to desks (endpoints), all updated from head office.
analogy.breaks: Directories update overnight; xDS updates in milliseconds.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Trace exactly how Envoy will route a request.

code.text:
istioctl proxy-config listeners cart-7d9.shop --port 8080
istioctl proxy-config routes cart-7d9.shop --name 8080 -o json | jq '.[0].virtualHosts[0].routes[0].route'
istioctl proxy-config endpoints cart-7d9.shop --cluster 'outbound|80||payments.shop.svc.cluster.local'

check.q: Which xDS API carries the actual pod IPs for a service?

identity-spiffe-ids.core: IP addresses are ephemeral in Kubernetes, so they're useless as identity. SPIFFE defines workload identity as a URI such as spiffe://cluster.local/ns/shop/sa/payments, derived from the Kubernetes service account, carried in short-lived X.509 certificates (SVIDs). The mesh CA issues and rotates them automatically, and policies say 'only cart may call payments' rather than referring to IP ranges.

first_principles.problem: Network policies based on pod IPs break whenever pods reschedule.

analogy.title: Employee ID badges instead of desk numbers
analogy.story: People move desks daily; their badge proves who they are wherever they sit.
analogy.breaks: Badges last years; SVIDs expire in hours, by design.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Only cart's identity can POST /charge, wherever pods run.

check.a: To limit damage from key theft and avoid manual revocation; automatic rotation replaces them frequently.

security-mutual-tls-mtls.core: In mutual TLS both sides present certificates: the client verifies the server's identity and the server verifies the client's. Meshes make it automatic: sidecars originate and terminate mTLS using SVIDs, so all service-to-service traffic is encrypted and authenticated without app changes. Use PERMISSIVE mode (accept both plaintext and mTLS) during migration, then STRICT (mTLS only).

first_principles.problem: Internal traffic is plaintext, and a compromised pod can sniff or impersonate other services.
truths: Both sides need proof of identity.
Migration must avoid breaking non-mesh clients.

analogy.title: Two spies exchanging verified passwords
analogy.story: Each must prove who they are before speaking, and the conversation is in code.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Plaintext connections to shop namespace rejected.

check.a: So services without sidecars can still connect while you roll out the mesh, avoiding outages before enforcing STRICT.

traffic-management-canary-deployments-tr.core: Because every request passes through a proxy, the mesh can route by weight (send 5% to v2), by header (beta users to v2), or mirror traffic (copy requests to v2 and discard responses). It can also inject faults (delays, errors) for resilience testing and apply retries, timeouts and circuit breaking. Canary releases shift weights gradually while watching error and latency SLOs, and tools like Flagger and Argo Rollouts automate this.

first_principles.problem: A risky release must reach 1% of users first, with automatic rollback if errors rise.

analogy.title: Opening one checkout lane with a new till system
analogy.story: Send a few customers through it; if it jams, close it and everyone uses the old tills.
analogy.breaks: Shops can watch the till; meshes rely on metrics thresholds.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Beta users and 5% of others hit v2.

check.a: Sends a copy of live requests to another version, discarding its responses, to test it with real traffic without user impact.

observability-the-three-pillars-in-a-mes.core: Proxies see every request, so a mesh produces uniform telemetry with no code changes. Metrics (request rate, errors and latency histograms per source and destination: golden signals in Prometheus), access logs, and distributed traces (spans per hop, as long as apps propagate trace headers such as traceparent). Tools like Kiali visualise the service graph, and the main gap is that apps must still forward trace context.

first_principles.problem: Each service team emits different metrics, and nobody can see the full request path during incidents.

analogy.title: Toll booths recording every car
analogy.story: Every booth logs cars, speeds and routes, so you can see traffic patterns across the whole network.
analogy.breaks: Toll booths read plates automatically; traces need apps to pass the 'plate' along.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Error rate for any service, uniformly.

check.q: Why do apps still need changes for full distributed tracing in a mesh?
check.a: Proxies create spans, but apps must forward trace headers from inbound to outbound requests so spans link into one trace.

the-ebpf-based-mesh-cilium.core: Sidecars cost resources per pod. Cilium moves much of the mesh into the kernel with eBPF: L3/L4 load balancing, network policy, identity-aware filtering and transparent encryption (WireGuard or IPsec) run without proxies, and L7 features use a shared per-node Envoy only when needed. Istio's ambient mode takes a similar sidecarless path with per-node ztunnels and optional waypoint proxies.

first_principles.problem: Sidecars consume 30% of cluster memory across 3,000 pods.
truths: L7 can be shared per node.
derivation: Use **per-node Envoy** for L7 only where needed.

analogy.title: Building-wide security system vs a guard per office
analogy.story: Cameras and badge readers built into the building replace a guard at every door; specialists are called only when needed.
analogy.breaks: Building systems are shared; kernel bugs affect all pods on a node.

check.q: How does a sidecarless mesh still provide L7 features?
check.a: By sending traffic that needs L7 processing through shared per-node or per-namespace proxies (Cilium's Envoy, Istio waypoints).
